title: The Disputed Tradeline: How DU, FHA TOTAL and a Manual Underwrite Each Treat a Consumer Dispute, and Where an AI Underwriting Agent Has to Stop
summary: A dispute flag on a credit tradeline changes how Fannie Mae's DU runs the loan, can force an FHA loan to a manual underwrite at $1,000 in disputed derogatory balances, and puts the lender between a borrower's FCRA rights and the agency rules. A technical account of how our agents find disputes on a tri-merge report, run the program tests, and what they will not do, which is coach a borrower to remove a dispute or decide whether it is valid.
body_markdown:
## Who This Is For


Underwriting managers, credit policy owners and the processors who clear credit conditions at lenders delivering to Fannie Mae and insuring with FHA. Also compliance officers who need to know what an AI agent is allowed to say to a borrower about their own credit report.


## Why a Dispute Flag Matters to an Underwriter


When a consumer disputes an account with a credit bureau, the bureau has 30 days to reinvestigate under[15 U.S.C. 1681i(a)(1)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681i) , and a furnisher that has been told of the dispute may not keep reporting the account without noting that it is disputed, under[15 U.S.C. 1681s-2(a)(3)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681s-2) . In Metro 2 reporting, that note is a compliance condition code: XB while the investigation is open, XC when it is complete and the consumer still disagrees, XH when a previously disputed account has been resolved.


The scoring models generally leave out disputed accounts while the flag is on, so a dispute can lift a score that the borrower's actual history does not support. That is why the agency rules treat a disputed tradeline as a question to be answered, not as a neutral fact on the report. And because the dispute may be completely legitimate, an identity theft or a reporting error, they also do not treat it as derogatory on its own.


## Fannie Mae: DU Runs the Loan Twice


[Selling Guide B3-5.3-09, DU Credit Report Analysis](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-5.3-09/du-credit-report-analysis) , describes a two-pass approach. DU first assesses the loan casefile using all tradelines, including the disputed ones. If that pass returns Approve/Eligible, no further documentation is needed for the disputes, and DU says so in its findings.


If the first pass does not approve, DU assesses the risk again without the disputed tradelines and issues a message listing them. The lender then has to find out whether the disputed information is accurate. If the borrower is not responsible for the account, the lender documents that and can deliver the loan as a DU loan. If the information turns out to be accurate, the recommendation that depended on leaving it out no longer stands: the lender needs a new credit report reflecting the corrected data and a resubmission, or the loan has to be manually underwritten under[B3-5.2-03](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-5.2-03/accuracy-credit-information-credit-report) , where Fannie expects a letter from the borrower explaining the dispute when there are several disputed accounts or a disputed mortgage tradeline. Disputed medical tradelines are left out of the DU message, so the lender does not have to investigate them.


The structure matters for automation. The DU message is the trigger, not the dispute flag itself. A loan with three disputed tradelines that approves on the first pass needs nothing. A loan with one disputed tradeline that only approves on the second pass needs an investigation, and the outcome of that investigation can change the recommendation.


## FHA: The $1,000 Downgrade


FHA's rule in Handbook 4000.1 for loans scored by the TOTAL Mortgage Scorecard is a dollar threshold. If the credit report shows the borrower has $1,000 or more in total disputed derogatory credit accounts, the loan must be downgraded to a Refer and manually underwritten. A disputed derogatory account means a disputed charge-off, a disputed collection, or a disputed account with late payments in the last 24 months. Disputed medical accounts do not count toward the $1,000, and neither does disputed derogatory credit from identity theft, credit card theft or unauthorized use, provided the lender documents it with a police report or the creditor's documentation. A disputed account with a zero balance does not trigger the downgrade. The rule has been in place since[Mortgagee Letter 2013-24](https://www.hud.gov/sites/documents/13-24ml.pdf) .


On a manual underwrite, the borrower has to provide a letter of explanation and documentation supporting the basis of the dispute, and the underwriter has to judge whether the explanation is consistent with the rest of the credit file.


So an FHA borrower with a disputed $640 collection and a disputed $410 charge-off (illustrative numbers) has crossed the threshold even though DU would have treated the same file differently, and a TOTAL Accept on that file is not one the lender can rely on.


## The Calculation People Get Wrong


When we built the credit checks in our[Conditions Manager](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/conditions-manager) , the disputed-tradeline logic was where we found the most variation in how human teams applied the same rule. The FHA test is a sum, and three things go wrong in it.


The first is the population. The sum is over disputed derogatory accounts, so a disputed account that is current and has never been late is out, and a disputed account with a single 30-day late 20 months ago is in. A processor scanning for "disputed" and adding every balance gets the wrong number.


The second is the exclusions. Medical accounts come out of the sum, which means the agent has to classify the creditor, and a medical debt sold to a general collection agency often loses the word "medical" on the report. Identity theft exclusions come out only with the documentation in the file.


The third is the report. A tri-merge report can show an account as disputed at one bureau and not at the others, and the same collection can appear twice under the original creditor and the collector. Counting both overstates the total. Counting neither because the bureaus disagree understates it.


Our agent reads the tradeline-level data from the credit report, not the summary page, and builds the disputed-derogatory list with each account's balance, status, bureau and the reason it was included or excluded, so the underwriter sees the sum and how it was built. Duplicates across bureaus are merged on account number and creditor before summing, and a merge the agent is not confident about stays as two lines with a note. Each result runs through[Triple Check](https://www.seiright.com/how-it-works#triple-check) , and anything below threshold becomes a named exception rather than a guessed number.


## What the Agent Will Not Do


There is a well-known shortcut in mortgage lending: ask the borrower to call the bureau and withdraw the dispute, then re-pull credit. Sometimes that is the right outcome, because the dispute was filed years ago, resolved, and never cleared. Sometimes it is wrong, because the borrower's dispute is valid, and asking them to withdraw it to get a loan approved means asking them to give up a right under the FCRA so that a score drops and a rule is satisfied.


We decided early that no agent of ours tells a borrower to remove a dispute. The[Document Concierge](https://www.seiright.com/for-lenders/document-concierge) can tell a borrower that an account on their report is marked as disputed, ask for their letter of explanation and supporting documents when the program requires them, and explain what happens next. Whether to ask the borrower to resolve or withdraw a dispute is a conversation for a loan officer or underwriter, who can judge the borrower's situation and is accountable for the advice. A borrower who withdraws a valid dispute because an automated message implied they had to is a UDAAP problem in waiting, and our post on[UDAAP and AI agents](https://www.seiright.com/blog/udaap-ai-agents-consumer-finance-cfpb-1031-1036) covers why the line on misleading implication sits lower than many teams expect.


The agent also does not decide whether a dispute is valid. It can point out that a letter of explanation says an account was never the borrower's while the same account appears on a bank statement with payments going to it. That inconsistency goes to the underwriter as evidence. The judgement stays with the underwriter, and if the loan is declined, the borrower gets the notice and reasons the[adverse action rules](https://www.seiright.com/blog/adverse-action-notices-ai-credit-decisions-ecoa-reg-b) require.


## Re-Pulls and the Fresh Report


Disputes also move. An XB flag can turn into XH between the initial credit pull and a re-pull for an expired report or a rescore, and the DU or TOTAL result can change with it. Every credit report in the file is a separate, dated record in the[Loan Graph](https://www.seiright.com/platform/loan-graph) , and the agent re-runs the dispute tests on each one rather than carrying forward the first answer. If the disputed-derogatory total crosses $1,000 on an FHA file between pulls, the Conditions Manager reopens the file as a manual underwrite with both reports cited, and our post on[credit monitoring between application and closing](https://www.seiright.com/blog/fresh-credit-undisclosed-debt-monitoring-ai-mortgage-permissible-purpose-fcra) covers the permissible-purpose side of those re-pulls.


A disputed tradeline is a small item on a large report. It is also where an automated underwriting result can depend on a fact nobody has checked, and where the fastest fix for the lender can cost the borrower a right. The rules for each program are specific enough to automate. Advising the borrower on what to do about their own dispute is a decision we leave with people.
